title: Shakti as a philosophy
hook: a hymn in the Rig Veda where a goddess speaks in the first person: I move with the gods, I bend the bow, I breathe out like the wind

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakti as a philosophy in a poet's bow: Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined like a word and its meaning. Did your words and your meaning match? Day one thousand eighty-nine.

I. A hymn can be sung to Agni, to Indra, to the dawn. This one in the Rig Veda is sung by someone. The speaker is Vak, a goddess whose name means speech, and tradition names her as the seer of the hymn herself. The whole hymn comes from her own mouth. I move with the gods. I hold them up. I bend the bow. I breathe out like the wind. This whole stretch of the path has been asking what Shakti is, through a verse, a straw, a seeing, a dancer, a question, a poet's bow. Today, the last day on Shakti as a philosophy, a Vedic hymn answers in the first person.
screen: `NOT SUNG TO HER. SUNG BY HER.` → `VAK: THE GODDESS WHO IS SPEECH.` → `SHE SPEAKS AS I.`

segments.voice: Here is some of the hymn, in paraphrase. I move with the Rudras and the Vasus, with the Adityas and all the gods. I hold up Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni. I am the queen, the gatherer of treasures. Through me eats the one who eats, the one who sees, breathes and hears. Without knowing it, they live in me. I bend the bow for Rudra. I breathe out like the wind, taking hold of all the worlds. Beyond the sky, beyond this earth: so great have I become. First, she holds the gods up. Not the other way around. The gods move because she moves with them. That's the Saundarya Lahari's Shiva who couldn't stir, in another key. Second, she is inside ordinary acts. Eating, seeing, breathing, hearing. Whoever does those, the hymn says, does them through her, without knowing it. That's the Shvetashvatara's hidden power, hidden in plain breath. Third, she arms the god. She bends the bow for Rudra, the fierce one. Power here is not gentle only. It defends. Fourth, and the widest: she breathes out like the wind and holds all the worlds, and then she says she has gone beyond the sky and the earth. Inside everything, and beyond it. Put that beside the Devi Upanishad's answer, I am Brahman, and you can hear why some in goddess traditions hold this hymn close. In their reading, power isn't something the divine has. It's what the divine is, when it speaks for itself. Tomorrow the path turns to another Vedic hymn to a goddess, this time sung to her: the Sri Sukta.
screen: `I MOVE WITH THE GODS. I HOLD THEM UP.` · `THROUGH ME, THEY EAT, SEE, BREATHE.` · `I BEND THE BOW FOR RUDRA.` · `INSIDE EVERYTHING, AND BEYOND IT.` · then, large: `I BREATHE OUT LIKE THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: through me. Sit, and let the breath come on its own. Notice it as the hymn does: something breathing through you, not only something you do. Then add the other acts from the verse, one at a time. Hearing: the sounds in the room, arriving without effort. Seeing: light on the closed eyelids, or the room if the eyes are open. Breathing: the out-breath, like the wind. Rest in all of it at once. If you pray, you can hold the word Devi, or Ma, with the out-breath. If you don't, just rest in the breathing. The bell holds the time.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Rig Veda, Vak speaks for herself: through her the world eats, sees, breathes and hears, and she breathes out like the wind.
Your line: Shakti as a philosophy. Today, at one meal, eat the first bite slowly, and notice the eating happening through you. Day one thousand eighty-nine.

howItsDone: This hymn, Rig Veda 10.125, is known as the Devi Sukta or Vak Sukta; it is chanted in goddess worship, and some recite it alongside the Devi Mahatmya.

fork.setup: you're Vak, and you're asked to describe yourself. which line is yours?
options: I serve the gods and wait for their orders.
I move with the gods, and I hold them up.
I live far from the world, above the sky only.
fork.reveal: I move with the gods, and I hold them up, she says. then she adds: I breathe out like the wind, and I've grown beyond sky and earth.

original.note: Sanskrit: vak, speech; the goddess who speaks Rig Veda 10.125 in her own voice.

what it means: here the goddess talks: she holds up the gods, lives in every breath, and reaches beyond the sky.

notes: Rig Veda 10.125 paraphrased (verses 1, 3, 4, 6, 8). Griffith 1896 is public domain but not on the validator's list, so nothing is quoted. Confirm 'I am the queen, the gatherer of treasures' (ahaṃ rāṣṭrī saṃgamanī vasūnām, 10.125.3) and 'so great have I become' (etāvatī mahinā saṃ babhūva, 10.125.8).
Seer attribution (Vāk Āmbhṛṇī) kept as 'tradition names'. 'Rudra, the fierce one': the link to Shiva was cut under the claims rule.
Last Shakti-as-a-philosophy day; the teach names tomorrow's Sri Sukta without teaching it.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced 'most hymns are sung to someone'; 'every line starts from her own mouth' and the screen 'every line begins with I' were not literally true and became 'the whole hymn comes from her own mouth' / 'she speaks as I'; the closing 'power is what the divine is' is now attributed to some in goddess traditions rather than said by the narrator.
